These generic overrides are for when the user knows what the element is going to be and needs access to special properties or methods on the HTML element. It is probably going to be pretty rare, but may be required in rare circumstances (maybe a hacked file upload that requires an `HTMLInputElement` type.

The fallback for all generic overrides is `HTMLElement` which contains all the generic methods and properties. Also the `Subject` returned by all Element selectors is a `JQuery` object which helps to normalize a lot of calls.

A way of getting the right element without using a generic would be to use the `.filter` method:

```ts
cy.get('.input') // HTMLElement since we can't infer type
  .filter('input') // HTMLInputElement since 'input' is a keyof match
  .then($input => {
    $el // $ExpectType JQuery<HTMLInputElement>
  })
```

That would also always make sure you have an `<input>` or else the test will fail before it gets there. I prefer this over generic overrides since overriding generics is basically overriding the type system (possible runtime error in that case)

I wonder if, given that info, that should be the way to get a specific element type? I don't like seeing generics in non-library code - it is just too easy to misuse.

Generics would still be required in areas we can't infer based on input (like fixture contents or results from a `.as`).
We can't narrow the type down much with a `.not`. I'm not even sure a generic should be used here. `HTMLElement` is what all elements would have in common. I think I'll remove the generic from this.

I added `ChainableArray<Subject>` to properly capture types for `.each` and `.spread` and theoretically any Command that is meant to work on arrays. Without this, `.each` and `.spread` would be forced to resort to `any` for parameters, putting more type burden on the application author.

The `Omit` part basically takes the whole `Chainable` interface and removes some keys ('and', 'as', etc in this case). I'm defining the `ChainableArray` interface to be the same as `Chainable` except a few methods are replaced with different type definitions. Without knowing much about Node.js streams or what is actually replaced here, I wonder how are replacements handled that fall over the chunk boundary?

`tail`, `replacement`, and `chunk` are all JS strings that consist only of complete Unicode graphemes (thanks to `utf8-stream` and `grapheme-splitter`), so by concatting/replacing with them there should not be any character boundary issues.

I'm not talking about splitting Unicode graphemes on the chunk boundaries, I'm talking about the string replacement here. If the matching string has the first half in one chunk and the second half in the next, the `tail.replace(pattern, replacement)` won't find it. 'chunk boundary friendliness' is one of the features of the original _replacestream_ library.

If you check out [`replacestream`'s options](https://github.com/eugeneware/replacestream#list-of-options), the `maxMatchLen` option controls the maximum length of the buffer to do replacements in. Here, `tail` is that buffer. This should work across cross-chunk boundaries in a similar way to `replacestream` by holding a buffer of `maxTailLength` size back.

It feels like part of the responsibly of a loader is to provide a scrim over the appropriate content. This can either be the entire viewport (fullscreen) or any element (non-fullscreen). However, in both cases, it prevents the user from taking action until after the loader has completed. This seems like the intended purpose of a loading screen/loader.

I am not suggesting to bake into `Loader` a scrim. The concept of a scrim stands on its own. However, we can leverage a Scrim (ui-block, etc.) and compose it within `Loader`.

Specifically, my suggestions are:
- compose Loader with a scrim (or ui-block; doesn't have be named Scrim)
- full screen loaders show a scrim the entire viewport
- non-full screen loaders show a scrim over their parent consumer
    - if we simply do not need a non-full screen loader, then consider naming this `FullScreenLoader` instead. If we come back in the future with a need for a non-fullscreen version then it can simply compose the `FullScreenLoader` within it.

Note: I would defer the non-fullscreen loader if possible; as it is more complicated in terms of implementation.

Edit: It appears like there is at least [one usage](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/3268/files#diff-2f9b8415c2aa516569e9ba1e934f198cR60) of a non-fullscreen loader.

It's not the *most* important thing, but still, in this PR we have a chance to...

* maintain a consistent user experience,
* have well-defined retry behavior around an error-prone section of code,
* avoid introducing new dependencies since we already have this functionality in createRetryingSocket,
* and reduce confusion/technical debt around this code section instead of adding new complexity and external libraries that developers have to understand

If we don't do it before this PR gets merged, it just becomes even more tech debt, and this code is only a few months old so we should try to keep it in nice shape for as long as possible.

I can implement it if you like since I already know the APIs involved, just let me know.

Be my guest and change it.
I would prefer using off the shelf 3rd party libs for this, since they are well tested. I also don't find the argument for introducing technical debt convincing. We will do more stuff in the retry function:
- connect to socket
- `CRI.List`
- check if the list contains the blank page

If the check fails, we are going to go ... and connect back to the socket? What if we just need more time ... to get `CRI.List` to query the tabs AFTER the connection? Will we get into a loop where we are not solving the problem? 

Right now it seems to me the retries are split where they need to be and are isolated.

You raise a good point re: reconnecting to the socket on each retry, that probably shouldn't happen.

I still think that it's important to preserve the retry messaging. Otherwise the error experience will look like this:

```
Retrying 20/33...
Retrying 21/33...
Failed to connect to browser
```

...then the user is left head-scratching, "why didn't it just retry like it said it was going to?" and we'll have to fix it later on...

So maybe we can keep pRetry and then move the "warning message" into a function that keeps track of how many times it's retried, so we can use it in both places when a retry occurs.

```html
<shadow-root>
```

```js
 	cy.get('bar')
```

No, you still need to pass the option to get `bar` without enabling it at a higher level (test config, cypress.json, etc). The option is only in effect for the duration of the command.

So `cy.get('bar', { includeShadowDom: true })` outside the `within` could traverse through multiple shadow boundaries and find `bar`. However, `cy.within` does not persist the `includeShadowDom` behavior. It acts as it normally does and scopes queries inside so if there was another `bar` outside `foo`, it would not also be in the result of `cy.get('bar')`.

Windows's NTFS and FAT32 filesystems prohibit using `:` inside of a filename, which is why this separator character was chosen:

* https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file#naming-conventions
* https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filename#Comparison_of_filename_limitations

However, in Linux ext4 filesystem, it is perfectly fine to create a filename with a colon in it:

```
➜ ~ echo "foo" > test:file
➜ ~ cat test:file
foo
```

I think this reinforces the idea that this feature should be Windows-only, so we can *avoid* having to create additional logic to make paths containing colons still work.

Instead, you could define your prop interface, then pass a React component that receives all of those props and does something with it. In that scenario you'd be passing the actual React function (or class) instance.

Finally, if you do want to do "render props" (which is essentially what you've done), you probably want to wrap the functions in `useCallback`.

I want to emphasize that with how you have written this, I don't think any change is necessary, and the first two suggestions would only bring extremely minor performance fixes. I was more just commenting for learning purposes.

I figured this out just by creating lots of use cases and observing the output. Here's the use case this solves. Consider this example (note the viewport - 200x2000, kind of unrealistic use case, who has a device this shape? But still, good to test these things).

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/19196536/118740257-bcf56e00-b88e-11eb-922d-2a96bdafbb2b.png)

Without this CSS, the screenshot is like this. Note the default behvior of `cy.screenshot`, which is `cy.screenshot({ capture: 'fullPage' })` (as opposed to `cy.screenshot({ capture: 'viewport' })`.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/19196536/118740292-d696b580-b88e-11eb-90d0-06517f319761.png)

This is the desired output - scroll down the page, stitch together the screenshot:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/19196536/118740314-e57d6800-b88e-11eb-9826-efedf39c0c55.png).

We need `overflow: scroll` to be applied. If `overflow: scroll` is not applied, Cypress tries to scroll, take a screenshot, and stitch them together. That's why you end up with that weird duplicating behavior in the first image above.

`scroll: overflow` is only applied if you have a static height set - `height: 100%` won't work. By doing `min(100%, 100vh)` it will apply `height 100vh` to components with a height greater than the viewport (100%). This supports the desired behavior.

Initial render -> run effect + setState -> render again

After some time

@flotwig this is a nasty one. The explanation I can come up with is this: The socket.io parser [uses](https://github.com/socketio/socket.io-parser/blob/af1b23ca85fb64a0d7a050abd0362c5f632ce429/lib/is-binary.ts#L27) `instanceof ArrayBuffer` to check whether a part of the object to be encoded is an ArrayBuffer. Now the place where the ArrayBuffer coming from the real server response and the place where a stubbed ArrayBuffer response are constructed are not in the same scope and thus the prototype of the respective ArrayBuffers are not the same, i.e. `instanceof` returns `false` even though the object provided is an ArrayBuffer but from a different context (see https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/instanceof#instanceof_and_multiple_context_e.g._frames_or_windows). So if you just use merge here you get a very puzzling behaviour:

- if you intercept a binary response but do not touch the body, everything works as expected (ArrayBuffer is detected as binary from socket.io parser and encoded correspondingly)
- if you intercept a binary response and replace the body by another ArrayBuffer you construct inside of your e2e test, it is encoded as text and the Cypress server receives `{}` instead of the encoded binary content.

The possible solutions I see are:

- Create a new ArrayBuffer and deep copy the binary values (implemented in [utils.ts](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/16755/files#diff-b0318835d7e6e6b3346d8b261b8647d0848c58591e3242a87af81483cd52380b)). I'm not 100% sure though if the copying via `Uint8Array` works for all scenarios.
- Overwrite the prototype with [Object.setPrototypeOf](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/setPrototypeOf) (also implemented in [utils.ts](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/16755/files#diff-b0318835d7e6e6b3346d8b261b8647d0848c58591e3242a87af81483cd52380b))
- Write a [custom parser](https://socket.io/docs/v3/custom-parser/) for socket.io that for example uses `_.isArrayBuffer` instead of `instanceof`.

Please let me know what you prefer to do here (I tend to go for the second option) so that I can adapt my PR accordingly.

Thanks to this comment, I realized a lot of these exports are only used in `runner-shared` and was able to remove a few.

That aside, This is actually set up in a similar manner. There is two main scenarios to consider: 

## 1. Single files modules

Single files inside of `packages/runner-shared/src`). Examples are `dom.js` and `logger.js`. 

Each one of these has a single named export - for example:

```js
// packages/runner-shared/src/dom.js

/* implementation */

export const dom = {
  addBlackout,
  removeBlackouts,
  addElementBoxModelLayers,
  // many more functions
}
```

So when you do `export * from './dom'`, it's just the same as what you are suggesting - a namespaced module via the named export (in this case, `dom`). Instead of import and re-exporting, we just do it in one line.

Usage is:

```js
import { dom } from '@packages/runner-shared'`

dom.addBlackout()
```

So it is still namespaced. This same pattern is applied to all root level files. Not as jumbled as it might look.

## 2. Directories with multiple files

The other scenario is a directory, like `snapshot-controls`. It has three files:

```jsx
- index.js
- snapshot-controls.jsx
- snapshot-controls.spec.jsx
```

`index.js` simply exposes the module interface. In this case it exports 1 component, `<SnapshotControls>`. I am not sure name-spacing make much sense for a single component. We could do `<Snapshot.Controls />`, but it seems overkill (a `Snapshot` namespace for a single component?) 

Usage is:

```js
import { SnapshotControls, dom, logger } from 'packages/runner-shared`
```

Thoughts?

## 3. Exception

The main exception is the `studio` directory, which two components (`<Studio>` and `<StudioModals>`) and one singleton (`studioModel`). We could namespace these, but it feels a bit odd to have React components and a global singleton in the same namespace:

```jsx
import { Studio } from '@packages/runner-shared'

export function SomeComponent () {
  studio.studioModel(/* stuff */)
  
  return (
    <studio.StudioModals />
  )
}
```

An alternative would be two modules (one for components, so `<Studio.Modals>` and `<Studio.Controls>`, for example, and a completely separate one for the global singleton. This is probably the module thats breaks the current pattern, so not sure if it's a big deal. 

We could convert this file to have lots of imports and apply the same idea inside of `src/index.ts` instead, but the end result is the same - one applies namespacing in a single file, the other defers namespacing to the module directory (either via named export in a file like `dom.js` or an `index.js` file inside a directory). What do you think?

- `npm_config_https_proxy` and `npm_config_proxy` are used with both http and https requests if set

Unlike other projects, Cypress type definition should copy definition files(d.ts) and bundle them ourselves because of the clash of mocha and jest test functions(i.e. `it`, `describe`, etc.). For more info, #7194.

But when we do them, there are 2 copies of mocha and jquery inside our project. Because of that, they cause errors because of the duplicate definitions of global names. 

To avoid that, I had to find a way to comment out one of them. I decided to comment the files inside `node_modules/@types` folder. I did it with patch files added to the project. 

But the problem is that those patches are applied earlier than copying them to the `cli/types`. So, the copied version is the commented version. That's why I had to write code above. 

I also don't like this solution and thought about other solutions like below:

* Copy the definitions when it is built for production => It seems that there is no prod-build only script. I wasn't confident enough to handle production build script.
* Don't use patch and comment them out on post-install.js => It cannot remove the code inside `post-install.js`. It can comment out already-commented files (i.e. the code will be complicated.)
* Creating our own `CyMocha`, `CyJQuery` definition. => It was impossible because definitions are tightly coupled. Removing some of them cause unexpected problems. 

The conclusion was the code above. 

I also hate this. But it seems that this is the simplest solution unless we remove `mocha`, `chai` from Cypress or make them optional.

p.s. And this solution is not perfect because it can cause temporary build failures in some environments. For example, I have to build twice on my Ubuntu 20.04 to finish it because the build fails somehow for the type failures.

Why change these to multiple different tests inside of a single `it`? Previously, you could do `verify.it.only` and only run one test. Now you can only narrow it down to however many tests happen to be in an `it`.
Very true, I'll update. I have proper types coming for this in the next PR, alongside a little refactoring.

Before, each `verify.it` would load the spec file and verify the output for a single spec within it. However, many of these spec files contained more than one test, so there was a lot of redundant execution. 

With the conversion to a more typical e2e test, it seemed like overkill to reload and wait for the entire suite to finish to assert on a single test within it. So this instead loads the suite once, waits for it to finish once, and then performs all the assertions for each test in that suite (within a single `it`). With this we go from 85 suite loads to about 25, saving us quite a bit of test time.

I agree that the granularity of having individual `it`s and the ability to use `.skip`/`.only` was convenient.  I had attempted to get the best of both worlds by performing a single load `before` the individual `it`s, but my understanding is that will not be possible with upcoming session changes. Another option would have been to break up the specs so that there is less execution redundancy, but that would have left us with a 85 individual spec files to maintain (and the overhead for loading/running each one).

I think the current implementation is a fair balance between maintaining existing coverage and overall test performance, but any input is good to have on this strategy before more tests get migrated.

I read those 2 issues. And below are my opinions:

### About #7318

I think #19541 and #7318 are separate issues. #7318 wants to listen to `search` event with `cy.type('{enter}')`. But the problem is that [`search` event is not a standard event](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLInputElement/search_event) as @jennifer-shehane wrote in the issue. 

I guess we can ignore this in this PR.


### About #8267

Yes and no. 

There are 2 problems in #8267.

1. `cy.get('#button').focus().type('{enter}')` should trigger `click` event. => It's solved by #19726. 
2. `cy.get('#button').type('f')` should not send click event. => It's not solved and the debate isn't ended. 

As in [the comment of #8767](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/8267#issuecomment-743918524), we should decide the current behavior of `cy.type` first. 

It assumes that `click` is required before typing into an element. But as we all know, "click" isn't the only way to make elements get focus. 

I believe #8267 should be handled after the decision about this has been made.

When we start recursively inspecting objects, listing out their properties, this can include elements with references to objects like `window` and `document`. And in Chrome 99, when we iterate over the properties of `document.adoptedStyleSheets`, it throws an error.

Ultimately though, there's no reason we should be looking over every property of a `Document`. In the same way we already abort for HTMLElements above, I added an early exit for ShadowRoot and Document, returning a string of their HTML rather than recursively enumerating their properties. This should be a minor performance win, saving on hundreds of calls through `formatValue` in cases where we pass in `window`, `document` or other global-ish objects that aren't literal HTMLElements.

Radio button has 2 states: unchecked (empty circle), checked (filled circle). When you focus the empty radio button (unchecked) and press the space bar, it is filled (checked) and `click` event is sent. 

But when we press the space bar again, `click` event is not fired because the radio button is already checked. 

To make it clear, I've edited the code like below:

```js
// We're clicking here first to make the radio element checked.
cy.get(`#target-input-radio`).click().type(' ')

// item 0 is click event. It's fired because we want to make sure our radio button is checked.
cy.get('li').eq(1).should('have.text', 'keydown')
cy.get('li').eq(2).should('have.text', 'keypress')
cy.get('li').eq(3).should('have.text', 'keyup')

cy.get('#target-input-radio').should('be.checked')
```

Unlike Chrome, Firefox automatically sends `click` event. Because of that, when we remove `!` here, Chrome does not send a `click` event and Firefox sends click events twice. 

This is the code to prevent this.

and it gets trimmed down to

Tim and I came across this PR and we're going to have a followup on this. Basically the TLDR is that you cannot make modifications to the driver without those first going into `develop` and having extensive test coverage around them.

I recognize you made this change because our 10.x tests make use of this behavior - and you were trying to get the tests to pass - but changes to the `driver` are the most critical changes to be heavily scrutinized. They need multiple reviewers and extensive test coverage because this is a foundational product behavioral change. 

Effectively modifying the `driver` code as part of this PR ends up "masking" the change, and it was only surfaced due to merge conflicts that a different developer mentioned to me. The proper way to handle this would be to first make a separate PR into `develop` - landing that, and then merging that into `10.x`. No. we are not closing and reopening the watcher anymore.

There used to be 2 watchers that did virtually the same thing but with some discrepancies and conflicts (specially in CI.
- One watcher used to watch the current `cypress.config.js`
- The other watcher used to watch all potential config files 

When renaming `cypress.config.js` into `cypress.config.ts` changes would be dealt with twice and break in circle.

Now we only have one single watcher that looks at all files potential and real.
When a change is detected, that is where cypress changes behavior if it's real or potential. 
This way, no need to klankebang any new watcher and the change is guaranteed to run once.

This is the best way I could find to verify the generated `cypress.config.js` works. Each project has two variants:

1. `<project>-configured`
2. `<project>-unconfigured`


The `-configured` variant is ready to run - it has the valid `cypress.config.js`. We verify it is valid by actually running the project via a system test: https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/20306/files#diff-9a09b374d404587d6bc455d2e1989ca5637a2e8cabbca5be488050a71ccb94f7. If the config is invalid, the system test will fail.

The `-unconfigured` variant is used by the launchpad e2e test: https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/20306/files#diff-757686eab70fe8cb1974b1e8d3fcdbbd2fde3fde61420e9708efcbc740e3fa47R11-R19. We select an unconfigured project, configure it with launchpad, and finally verify the generated `cypress.config.js` we create is identical to the one in `-configured`, which we know works since we have a system test for it.

A bit of work involved, but this gives me confidence we are generating a config file that is proven to work correctly.

2. Try using esbuild if it exists via `require.resolve('esbuild')`

3. Try node's real esm loading logic via `await import(configFile)`

We're already using `current` to the get the `userInvocationStack`. It's guaranteed to be `switchToDomain` because we don't resolve `switchToDomain` until either the secondary queue finishes or there's an error, in which case the queue is stopped for good. 

One option is we could pass the userInvocationStack into the spec bridge with `run:domain:fn` and replace the stack before sending it back, then we don't need to worry about it when reifying the error. This also addresses your question about [this comment](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/blob/standardize_error_and_object_serialization/packages/driver/src/multi-domain/events/logs.ts#L16). I think that may be necessary because the logs bypass `switchToDomain` and go straight to the runner. Though now that I think about it, I'm not sure if we want the log to have the `userInvocationStack`, the original stack, or a combination of both. But no need to worry about that for right now. Just pointing out that this solution (passing the userInvocationStack to the spec bridge) may be needed for that use case as well.
